item.title: Why is the U.S. mad about who sells cheese in Canada?
item.description: Cheese has once again become a hot topic in the Canada-U.S. trade dispute. While officials work to lower sectoral tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum, the U.S. wants Canada to change its strict ...
item.dc:creator: Anam Khan
item.content:encoded: Cheese has once again become a hot topic in the Canada-U.S. trade dispute. While officials work to lower sectoral tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum, the U.S. wants Canada to change its strict rules on importing cheese, which a Canadian agricultural economist warns heavily against. “It’s not in the Canadian interest,” explains Al Mussell, a prominent Canadian agricultural economist and policy analyst. Last month, U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order threatening a 50 per cent tariff on Canada’s dairy sector, which is now in a three day suspension period as negotiations continue. Mussell explains that the U.S. wants more control over who can access Canadian retailers directly, so they can export some of their premium products to Canada. “Of course, that’s not how our system works,” he says, adding that allowing it would threaten Canadian processors and complicate the domestic raw milk allocation system. Canada currently gives dairy import quota access mainly to processors, while retailers are excluded under CUSMA. The U.S. argues that this restriction creates an unfair playing field because retailers are granted access under Canada’s trade agreement with the European Union. The U.S. administration says “Canada is discriminating against the commerce of the United States through Canada’s tariff-rate quota allocation measures imposed on U.S. cheeses of all types.” Canada and the U.S. have fought over this before The dispute over who gets access to Canada’s dairy quotas is not new. The U.S. first launched a formal dispute under CUSMA, arguing that Canada’s dairy import system shut out U.S. producers because it gave almost all its import permits to domestic dairy factories. After a trade panel ruled that this was unfair, Canada changed the rules to let other dairy businesses, like distributors, get the permits too. However, retailers remain excluded. When the U.S. challenged Canada again, arguing retailers should also be allowed direct access, the panel sided with Canada, saying it was in compliance with CUSMA. Mussell says the U.S. continuing to press the issue despite that ruling is not a good sign. “I think it goes far beyond cheese or dairy products,” he says. “When the President can come in and make threats that contravene a decision that the dispute panel under the CUSMA agreement rendered… that’s really troubling.” What happens if retailers get more access? Mussell says giving grocery retailers direct access would not increase the total amount of U.S. cheese entering Canada, since the quota is already essentially filled, but it could shift sales away from Canadian manufacturers. He says it could also complicate Canada’s supply management system because raw milk is allocated to processing plants on a regulated basis. “That could be costly to the Canadian dairy industry,” he says. Mussell also warns that giving grocery retailers more direct access to imports could strengthen their negotiating position with Canadian dairy suppliers. “Your’re kind of arming them in terms of the sorts of relations that they can have with their dairy suppliers,” he says. ‘Our national food sovereignty is not up for negotiation’ In response to the tariff threat, a joint letter by the Dairy Farmers of Canada and the Dairy Processors Association of Canada last week expressed disappointment that the dairy sector was dragged into a trade dispute once again. “Our national food sovereignty is not up for negotiation,” said David Wiens, president of DFC. “It is also clear that Canadians believe in the importance of having control over our food supply and ensuring that Canada’s strong domestic dairy sector is not compromised.” The trade relationship in dairy already “massively favours the U.S.” said Mathieu Frigon, president of the DPAC. “U.S. dairy exports to Canada far exceed Canadian dairy exports to the U.S. by more than $600 million annually and have increased by more than 150% since CUSMA came into effect,” said Frigon. What about the quality of U.S. dairy? Mussell says even if more U.S. milk entered Canada, there is a major difference between Canadian and U.S. dairy quality standards. “You could have milk that shipped under the U.S. Grade A that would not be saleable in any province in Canada,” he says. Moreover, he says a significant amount of American milk doesn’t even meet its own Grade A standard. “Is that product being exported to Canada, made from that milk? We don’t know. They don’t label. We have no way of knowing that,” says Mussell. He says federal funding for labs that monitor the U.S. milk testing system stopped last year. “What’s the nature of the safety and quality of product that we’re getting from the United States? I don’t know that we have an answer for that, and it’s concerning,” says Mussell.

item.title: Canada-U.S. trade minister arrives in Washington as premiers express optimism about possible deal. Live tariff updates here.
item.description: Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc has arrived in Washington for more talks after U.S. President Donald Trump chose to delay his new tariffs until later this week.
item.dc:creator: CTVNews.ca Staff
item.content:encoded: Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc has arrived in Washington for more talks after U.S. President Donald Trump chose to delay his new tariffs until later this week. LeBlanc and Chief Negotiator Janice Charette were seeing arriving shortly after noon ET at the U.S. Trade Representative offices to meet with their American counterpart Jamieson Greer. They were joined by Canada’s Ambassador to the U.S. Mark Wiseman and Prime Minister Mark Carney’s chief of staff Marc-André Blanchard. Canada and the U.S. now have until Saturday to reach a deal before Trump imposes 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian goods. In a Truth Social post Tuesday night, the U.S. president stated that he would delay his tariffs for three days and added that the two countries have reached a tentative deal. He also said that the Keystone XL pipeline “may be awoken from the grave.” Carney’s own statement released Wednesday did not mention a deal or a pipeline, but said that “substantial progress has been made.” Follow along for key updates: All provinces agreed to restock U.S. liquor: N.L. premier Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham says Canada’s premiers have agreed to return U.S. alcohol to store shelves as part of the tentative trade deal with the U.S. He said the prime minister is confident an agreement will be reached and that “as part of this agreement, he asked all of the provinces, as a sign of good faith, ‘would we put U.S. liquor back on our shelves,’ and we all agreed.” Several of the premiers have not commented publicly on the issue. U.S. alcohol products remain off the shelves in every province except Alberta and Saskatchewan. Tiffany Hendsbee, CTV News Supervising Multiplatform Writer Carney speaks with Quebec premier Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke with Quebec Premier Christine Frechette again today, a source with knowledge tells CTV News. It comes a day after Carney met with his cabinet and the country’s premiers following the news about a potential trade deal. Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist Sectoral tariffs reduced: sources Multiple sources tell CTV News there are reductions in sectoral tariffs, such as steel and aluminum, as part of the agreement with the United States, but none of the sources knew the scope of those reductions. As for how the public will respond, sources also tell CTV News the details of those sectorial tariffs will “make or break the deal” politically for Prime Minister Mark Carney. CTV News Ottawa Bureau ‘Can’t make a good deal with a bad person’: Manitoba’s Kinew Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew told Winnipeg’s 680 CJOB Thursday it looks like there will be a lower tariff on the Gerdau steel mill in Selkirk, Man., but it is still “way higher than it was two years ago.” Kinew added that Carney asked the provinces to return American booze to the shelves, and told them they could blame him if they receive any backlash for the decision. “If we do end up putting the booze back on the shelves, like I’ve said. we still have to see some of the details here, we reserve the right to take it back off again, because we know that this guy is very erratic, the American president, and he may go back on his word, as he’s done countless times,” Kinew said in his radio interview. The Manitoba premier also quoted famed investor Warren Buffett in saying “you can’t make a good deal with a bad person,” once again referring to Trump as “Jeffery Epstein’s best friend” and blaming the president for high gas prices brought on by the war in Iran. The Canadian Press, Read the full article here. ‘Sounds like Canada has given up’: Scheer Conservative House leader Andrew Scheer says although he’s “cautiously optimistic,” he is “worried” about what Carney may be giving to avoid 50 per cent tariffs. “My hope is that we get an elimination of tariffs. It sounds like Canada has given up,” Scheer told CTV Your Morning Saskatchewan Thursday morning. Scheer said the big question is whether Carney comes back with zero tariffs, or the baseline of 25 per cent. “If he comes back with a deal where there’s still 25 per cent tariffs on steel and aluminum, there’s going to be a lot of workers here in Regina (and) across the country that will be scratching their heads, saying, ‘You know, Mark Carney seems to have given up quite a lot.’” Scheer also echoed criticism raised by Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, saying Carney has failed to brief the Opposition on negotiations. “We’re in a little bit of a wait-and-see mode. We’ll see what the final deal is.” Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist Agriculture the ‘No. 1 issue’: U.S. secretary Brooke Rollins, the U.S. secretary of agriculture, says President Trump remains “very focused on Canada, specifically as it relates to dairy,” as well as other issues. Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Rollins said she and Trump believe the new deal will make farmers happy. “My great friend Scott Bessent … Howard Lutnick, (and) Jamieson Greer, they have made, alongside President Trump and with his direction, agriculture as the No. 1 issue as they are moving into these rooms and have these discussions” she said. “The president has not been shy about his frustration with Canada and especially with dairy and what Canada’s rules have done to our incredible dairy producers in America.” Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist Why is the U.S. mad about who sells cheese in Canada? Cheese has once again become a hot topic in the Canada-U.S. trade dispute. While officials work to lower sectoral tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum, the U.S. wants Canada to change its strict rules on importing cheese, which a Canadian agricultural economist warns heavily against. “It’s not in the Canadian interest,” explains Al Mussell, a prominent Canadian agricultural economist and policy analyst. Mussell explains that the U.S. wants more control over who can access Canadian retailers directly, so they can export some of their premium products to Canada. Last month, U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order threatening a 50 per cent tariff on Canadian goods, including the country’s dairy sector. Anam Khan, BNN Bloomberg journalist, Read the full article here. ‘In the end game’: diplomat Negotiations are nearing a close, Canada’s U.K. high commissioner says, judging from the joint statements given by Canadian and U.S. trade reps on the state of talks this week. Ralph Goodale, who is a member of the prime minister’s advisory council on Canada-U.S. economic relations, pointed to a media appearance by Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc and his U.S. counterpart Jamieson Greer on Wednesday in Washington. “The two of them together commenting on what they were presenting as a successful negotiation .... we’re very much in the end game,” Goodale told CTV News Channel on Thursday. Getting the premiers to agree on the deal may sound “impossible,” he added, if not for the display of “national cohesion” by Canadians. “That’s an incentive for all politicians ... to pull together,” he said. Yet, the “antipathy” developed towards the U.S. could still make it a “hard sell,” Goodale noted. “Canadians will be wary,” he acknowledged. “...The reliability of the arrangement is always going to be a question in Canadians’ minds.” Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist Keep the quota system: Dairy farmer A Quebec dairy farmer wants to keep the quota system used in Canada’s supply management “intact” in trade negotiations with the U.S. “We have a lot of money invested in that,” Angus MacKinnon told CTV News Channel on Thursday. Canadian dairy farmers produce supply according to quotas assigned by the federal government and are paid regulated pricing that factors in production costs, farm labour and capital expenditures. “The stability that quota brings to the dairy industry is reflected in the community,” MacKinnon said. The tariffs haven’t impacted income, he added. Last year Canada conceded four per cent of national production to the U.S. in trade talks but said it would not negotiate more on market access, he added. “I’m investing a tremendous amount of money in the construction of a barn,” he said. “So I need a positive outlook for the future.” Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist Softwood lumber is ‘outlier’ in trade talks: expert It’s still unclear how softwood lumber will be treated in ongoing trade negotiations, according to an industry expert. But Derek Nighbor, president and CEO of Forest Products Association of Canada says that he’s “optimistic.” The industry employs almost 200,000 people in Canada, “more than auto, steel and aluminum combined,” he told CTV News Channel on Thursday. “We’re still hopeful in the home stretch here,” he added. Ideally, Sections 338 and 232 which directly impact the industry would be eliminated, he said. “If we can see those tariffs go away and if we can get a commitment to see Canada and the United States get back to the table to negotiate an agreement on softwood, I think that would be a pretty good outcome,” he said. Under existing tariffs, the industry is losing market share to the Americans, Austrians, Swedes and Germans, as the Europeans only bear a 15 per cent premium, he said. “We’ve heard the president talk this week a lot about fairness and treating Canada more equally in different segments like other countries,” he said. “Lumber is clearly an outlier, and we’d like to see that gap close very much.” Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist Foreign affairs minister travels to Washington Anita Anand, Canada’s minister of foreign affairs, will travel to Washington on Thursday to meet her U.S. counterpart, Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Global Affairs Canada stated in a press release on Thursday that the two will discuss “continental security and other global priorities” but did not share more details. According to a Thursday schedule released by the U.S. Department of State, Anand will meet with Rubio at 1:30 p.m. EDT at the White House. The meeting will be closed to the media. Anand’s office has confirmed the meeting is not related to trade negotiations. Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist Premiers are optimistic Some premiers say they’re optimistic about Canada’s progress in reaching a trade deal to avoid punishing tariffs from the United States, while others say they’re waiting for more details about the agreement. Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston told reporters Wednesday that he was “optimistic” about the deal, adding that Prime Minister Mark Carney has asked provinces to restock American alcohol on their shelves. B.C.’s David Eby said that while no agreement will offer everything the country is hoping for, the federal government has made substantial progress across strategic sectors. Scott Moe of Saskatchewan said Wednesday that he hopes both countries can negotiate a deal that would reduce U.S. tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminum, autos and lumber. Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette told reporters it was too soon to make a judgment call about the deal, adding that she needed more information to see whether it’s positive for her province. The Canadian Press Province needs to diversify: N.S. premier Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston said that Canada’s trade dispute with the U.S. has been a wake-up call to diversify the province’s economy. Houston was responding late Wednesday to a potential Canada-U.S. trade deal from Banff, Alta., where he’s promoting energy projects at an industry conference. He said the dispute has taught the province it needs to develop more diverse trading partners for sectors like seafood and agriculture, though the U.S. market is still important. He said Nova Scotia also has to be more self-sufficient, especially on the energy file. “The whole experience has taught us something really important about diversification and pushing Nova Scotian opportunities,” Houston told reporters. " “That’s why I’m in Alberta right now talking about Nova Scotia gas and ... oil and ... opportunities. Diversifying our trading partners for our markets and seafood and agriculture and all kinds of things.” The Canadian Press, Read the full article here Reducing steel, aluminum tariffs ‘extremely important’: expert An international trade lawyer says an agreement that includes reductions to Section 232 tariffs on steel and aluminum will be “extremely important” for sectors that have been “really suffering.” “If we can regain access to the United States market, our producers are going to be in a much better place, and might even have a competitive advantage compared with the rest of the world,” William Pellerin told CTV News Channel on Thursday. While neither side has confirmed details involving dairy, comments made by Trump on Wednesday that the new agreement is “great for our farmers” leads Pellerin to suspect “minor concessions” have been made. Left off the negotiating table so far is softwood lumber, which Pellerin said is a disadvantage for Quebec, British Columbia and Alberta lumber producers. “It would have been nice relief, but I think we probably didn’t have enough cards to play to also get some relief on that sector,” he said. Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist Keystone XL benefits both: expert “It’s really one of those unique cases where I think both countries benefit,” said Dennis McConaghy, a former Canadian energy executive, on Thursday. In an interview with CTV Your Morning, McConaghy explained that Canada would benefit economically if Keystone XL were revived, since Canadian heavy oil suits U.S. refineries. “Now the argument has always been Canada might gain more economic margin by sending its incremental oil production to the West Coast,” McConaghy said. “Of course, that means you have to be able to get a pipeline built to the West Coast, and that’s always had obvious risks.” Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist Avoid ‘escalation’: agri-food expert Canada’s agri-food exporters are “optimistic” about Trump’s tariff pause as it abated a potential “escalatory spiral” that could have hurt business, a Canadian expert says. Michael Harvey, the executive director of the Canadian Agri-Food Trade Alliance, told CTV News Channel on Wednesday that while the industry isn’t directly impacted by the tariffs, there has been “an increasing level of political risk that’s made it difficult to make business decisions to invest.” “Our concern has been an escalatory spiral where there could be across-the-board tariffs that would hit,” he said. Despite becoming a more difficult market to work with, the U.S. still makes up 70 per cent of Canada’s agri-food exports, he added. “We have to manage these contradictory ... situations.” “Our situation is of confidence, but not too much confidence.” Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist PM Carney asks for return of U.S. booze Following a virtual first ministers meeting, Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston said Prime Minister Mark Carney asked the provincial leaders “to return the U.S. alcohol to the shelf.” In a virtual media conference on Wednesday, Houston said the ask is “something that came directly out of the negotiating table,” and is “something that (he) would be willing to do for the prime minister at this point in time.” “Whether Nova Scotians or whether Canadians will actually buy it when it gets back on the shelves, that’s a whole other discussion,” he added. Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist Provincial sources: trade deal not done Multiple provincial sources are sharing cautious optimism with CTV News following a briefing with Carney on the tentative trade deal between Canada and the U.S. However, they also emphasized that the deal is not done yet. In a post to Truth Social late Tuesday, Trump said the countries “have a deal,” but sources say that characterization is not accurate and further negotiations are ongoing. The provincial sources also tell CTV News that Carney personally asked the premiers to return U.S. alcohol to store shelves. He even told them he will bear any public pushback if that happens. According to a recent Nanos Research survey, most Canadians say they won’t purchase U.S. booze if it returns to stores. Stephanie Ha, bureau manager, Ottawa News Bureau With files from CTV News’ chief political correspondent Vassy Kapelos

item.title: Pressure builds anew in the bond market as Walmart drags the U.S. stock market lower
item.description: Asian shares advanced Thursday, tracking Wall Street gains, and South Korea’s benchmark Kospi jumped nearly six per cent.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: NEW YORK — A rise in oil prices on Thursday is sending worries about inflation and yields in the bond market higher, erasing some of the relief the U.S. Treasury Department created the day before. A drop for Walmart following its latest profit report also helped drag the U.S. stock market lower. The S&P 500 slipped 0.2 per cent and is on track for a fourth loss in the five days since setting its all-time high last week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 305 points, or 0.6 per cent, as of 9:35 a.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 0.3 per cent lower. The bond market remains the center of action after yields charged higher through the summer on worries about high inflation, gargantuan government debts and other factors. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent made a move Wednesday that jolted financial markets to at least double the size of his department’s planned purchases of longer-term Treasurys from Sept. 9 through Nov. 4. That helped push yields down after the 10-year Treasury’s yield had hit its highest level in more than a year and the 30-year yield got back to where it was in 2007, before the Great Recession sent yields toward zero worldwide. It’s a big deal because high yields slow the economy by raising interest payments for people, companies and the government and can undercut prices for stocks and other investments. But analysts had cautioned the effect may be short lived, given how small the purchases are relative to the overall size of the Treasury market and other factors. Plus, more signals arrived quickly to push the bond market’s worries higher. The U.S. government’s debt topped US$40 trillion on Wednesday, a staggering record that arrived just months after the national debt first blew past the US$39 trillion mark in April, because Washington continues to spend far more money than it brings in. And on Thursday, the price for a barrel of Brent crude climbed 2.4 per cent to US$93.83 as uncertainty continues about when the war with Iran will allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again. President Donald Trump threatened Iran with “Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale” late Wednesday but provided few details. That helped push the 10-year Treasury up to 4.69 per cent from 4.65 per cent late Wednesday. It’s almost back to its 4.71 per cent level from late Tuesday, before the Treasury Department made its announcement. A couple encouraging reports on the U.S. economy also helped push up longer-term Treasury yields, which move with expectations for the economy and inflation in coming years. One said fewer U.S. workers applied for unemployment benefits last week than economists expected, while another said manufacturing in the mid-Atlantic region appears to be much stronger than expected. On Wall Street, Walmart was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500 lower and fell 7.5 per cent even though it reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Investors focused more instead on how an important underlying measure of revenue growth at its stores slowed again. Its forecast for profit in the current quarter also fell short of analysts’ expectations. Advance Auto Parts tumbled 19.8 per cent after the retailer reported weaker revenue for the latest quarter, even though its profit topped expectations. CEO Shane O’Kelly said that “tighter household budgets constrained spending more than we anticipated, especially during the last four weeks of the quarter.” Helping to keep Wall Street’s losses in check was Deere, which reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It rose 3.6 per cent as the company said order trends indicate the agriculture equipment business looks set to accelerate after this year. In stock markets abroad, indexes dipped in Europe following a stronger finish in Asia. South Korea’s Kospi soared 5.9 per cent for one of the world’s biggest moves after the two tech titans that dominate its market, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, jumped. ___ Stan Choe, The Associated Press AP Business Writers Chan Ho-him and Michelle Chapman contributed to this report.

item.title: Corus makes cuts at Global BC, Global National, News 640 and talk radio
item.description: Corus Entertainment has made a “small number” of changes in select markets including jobs at Global BC, Global National, News 640 and talk radio.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — Corus Entertainment is making cuts at its TV and radio operations. A company spokesperson says it has made a “small number” of changes in select markets including jobs at Global BC, Global National, News 640 and talk radio. They say the changes are difficult but necessary to ensure its teams are structured in a sustainable way, while minimizing disruption to local news and audio delivery. The latest move comes after Corus cut dozens of jobs, mostly in Western Canada, earlier this year as part of programming changes across the country. Corus recently reported a net loss attributable to shareholders of $36.5 million in its third quarter, as its revenue for the period fell 16 per cent compared with a year earlier. The company is awaiting approval of its proposed recapitalization plan that would see lenders swap debt for equity in a new parent corporation. --- This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 20, 2026.
